bodyMarkdown:
Ferritin is a blood test that gives us a clue about your stored iron. It can be helpful when we are looking into fatigue, hair shedding, poor sleep, uncomfortable leg sensations, or other ongoing symptoms. Still, one ferritin result cannot diagnose the cause of every symptom by itself.

A result is usually reported in nanograms per milliliter, or ng/mL. This is numerically the same as micrograms per liter, or mcg/L. When we review [ferritin guidelines](/services/), we also look at your symptoms, complete blood count, transferrin saturation, inflammation, medications, diet, and health history.

Recent attention around a ferritin level of 16 has led to understandable questions. Why might one clinician mention 16, while a dermatologist discusses a different range and restless legs syndrome guidance mentions a much higher number? These thresholds can serve different purposes. A cutoff used to identify likely low iron stores is not always the same as a treatment threshold for a specific condition.

## **Why the 16 Cutoff Matters in [Ferritin Guidelines](/services/)**

In some [ferritin guidelines](/services/), a level below 16 may point to likely low or depleted iron stores in otherwise healthy people. This can matter because iron deficiency may be present before anemia shows up on a complete blood count. In other words, a normal hemoglobin result does not always answer every iron-related question.

The number 16 is best understood as a possible diagnostic signal, not a universal goal. A clinician may use it to help identify possible iron deficiency, then consider the full picture before deciding what it means for you.

It helps to separate four ideas:

* A diagnostic cutoff may help identify probable low iron stores.
* A treatment threshold may be higher for a particular condition or symptom pattern.
* A personal target, if treatment is appropriate, depends on your health history and follow-up testing.
* A ferritin number alone does not explain why iron stores may be low.

Ferritin also has limits. It can rise with inflammation, infection, liver concerns, and other health conditions. That means a ferritin result above 16 does not always rule out an iron-related concern, especially when inflammation is present. On the other hand, a level below 16 deserves thoughtful follow-up rather than an assumption that supplements are the only answer.

## **Ferritin in Dermatology Discussions**

Hair shedding and thinning are common reasons ferritin comes up in dermatology visits. Low iron stores can be one factor worth considering when someone has diffuse shedding or a pattern that may resemble telogen effluvium. Yet iron status is only one piece of a much larger hair-health puzzle.

Dermatology does not have one universally accepted ferritin target for every type of hair concern. Some clinicians may view low ferritin as relevant in a hair shedding workup. Others may place more weight on the pattern of hair loss, scalp findings, thyroid markers, hormone changes, nutritional status, medications, recent illness, and major stressors.

For that reason, we do not recommend assuming that raising ferritin to a certain number will automatically lead to hair regrowth. Correcting confirmed iron deficiency may be appropriate for some people, but it is not a guaranteed answer for every dermatologic symptom. Hair changes often have more than one contributor, and the right plan depends on the full clinical picture.

## **RLS Guidance Uses Different Iron Thresholds**

Restless legs syndrome, often called RLS, is a neurologic condition that causes an urge to move the legs. Symptoms often become more noticeable during rest, in the evening, or at night. Some people describe crawling, pulling, aching, or uncomfortable sensations that improve temporarily with movement.

Iron testing is especially important in RLS because brain iron availability may play a role in symptoms, even when anemia is not present. In its review of restless legs syndrome, JAMA discusses iron assessment as part of care. Current specialty guidance also recognizes that treatment decisions for RLS may use thresholds well above a ferritin level of 16.

For people with possible RLS, clinicians may consider iron treatment when ferritin is 75 ng/mL or lower or when transferrin saturation is below 20%. That does not mean everyone with ferritin below 75 has iron deficiency or needs iron treatment. It means RLS has its own condition-specific approach.

A careful RLS review may include:

* Ferritin, transferrin saturation, and complete blood count findings
* Sleep quality and other possible causes of disrupted sleep
* Medications that may worsen leg symptoms
* Kidney function and pregnancy status when relevant
* Other causes of uncomfortable leg sensations or nighttime movement

This is why an RLS treatment threshold should not be treated as a universal ferritin guideline for every person or symptom.

## **Check Inflammation and Iron Markers Before Making Decisions**

Ferritin is known as an acute-phase reactant. Put simply, inflammation can make ferritin appear normal or high even when the body does not have enough available iron. This can be especially relevant for people living with chronic, complex, or autoimmune-related health concerns.

When we review iron status in our remote care model, we look beyond a single lab value whenever appropriate. Depending on your situation, a clinician may consider a complete blood count, serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, transferrin saturation, and inflammatory markers. Each test offers a different clue, and none should be read in isolation.

Iron supplements also deserve caution. They can cause side effects and may not be appropriate for people with iron overload disorders, certain liver concerns, or other medical conditions. Before using high-dose iron products, it is important to review possible blood loss, absorption challenges, diet, medications, and the reason your iron markers may be abnormal. See also [how SIBO, iron pills, and birth control can affect iron](/how-sibo-iron-pills-and-birth-control-affect-iron/) and [root causes of anemia and low ferritin](/root-causes-of-anemia-and-low-ferritin/).

## **Use Your Results to Plan a Thoughtful Next Step**

The 16 cutoff can be a useful signal, but it is only one part of ferritin interpretation. Hair concerns, RLS symptoms, inflammation, and possible iron deficiency each call for a different clinical lens. Bringing prior lab results, a symptom timeline, medication list, dietary patterns, and relevant health history to your appointment can make that conversation more useful.

The most helpful next step is usually not chasing one number. It is understanding what your ferritin result may mean in the context of your body, symptoms, and other iron markers. This article is for educational purposes only and does not replace individualized medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.
